title: Social media and the tongue
hook: the adab of speech applies online too

segments.voice: Yesterday, technology and worship, and a patterned garment handed back. Your line was real presence. Where did you leave the phone, and what did you notice without it? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-three.

Here's a question the early Muslims never had to ask. Does backbiting count if you type it instead of saying it? Does passing on a rumor count if all you did was tap share? Does a cruel comment under a stranger's photo count, if the stranger never reads it? The sayings about speech come from a world of rooms, doorways and roads, where a listener usually stood in front of the speaker. Now a word can travel to a crowd of screens before the person who wrote it has put the phone down. Today takes the old manners of the tongue, what Muslims call adab, and carries them online.
screen: `DOES IT COUNT IF YOU TYPE IT?` → `WORDS ONCE HAD A FACE IN FRONT OF THEM.` → `THE ADAB OF SPEECH, ONLINE.`

segments.voice: Start with the plainest rule. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good, or keep silent. Two choices. Good, or nothing. There's no third box marked technically true but unkind. Then the second report, also in al-Bukhari: a Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand other Muslims are safe. Tongue and hand, side by side. Once, those were two different things. Now, on a phone, the hand does the talking. The thumbs are the tongue. Third, the rumor. Imam Muslim, in the introduction to his collection, keeps a saying that it is enough of a lie for a person to pass on everything he hears. Not inventing anything. Just passing it on. And the Qur'an itself, in the chapter called The Private Apartments, asks the believers to check a report brought by someone untrustworthy before acting on it, so that they don't harm people in ignorance and regret it afterward. A few verses later, the same chapter forbids backbiting, and asks, in a picture that's hard to forget, whether any of you would love to eat the flesh of a dead brother. So put the four together and hold them up to a screen. Say good or stay quiet. Let your hand be as safe as your tongue. Don't pass on everything that reaches you. Check it before you act on it. None of these rules mentions a phone, and every one of them fits on one. This week began with scholars saying no to extremism and with every soul sacred. It moved through friendship, hate answered with good, a heart healed two ways, and real presence. Much of it, in the end, came down to words.
screen: `SAY GOOD, OR KEEP SILENT.` · `THE TONGUE AND THE HAND, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `DON'T PASS ON EVERYTHING YOU HEAR.` · `CHECK THE REPORT FIRST.` · then, large: `THE THUMBS ARE THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at your thumbs. Really look at them, resting in your lap or on the table. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last few things you typed to anyone, a message, a comment, a post. Don't judge them yet. Just let them come up, one at a time. For each one, ask the hadith's question: was it good, or would silence have been better? If one stings a little, notice it, and let it go with the breath. Then think of one thing you might type today, and run it through the same question before it's written. If you pray, you can ask for a careful tongue. The bell holds the time.
Social media and the tongue. The old manners of speech, say good or stay silent, check before you pass it on, carried into every post and comment. Today's word.
screen: `SOCIAL MEDIA AND THE TONGUE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the tongue has thumbs. Today, post nothing unkind, and before you share anything, ask whether you know it's true. Tomorrow, moon sighting debates. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Some Muslim teachers apply the hadith on speech, say good or keep silent, to messaging and social media, and some Muslims make a habit of checking a story before they share it.

match.prompt: the manners of the tongue — tap the pairs.
pairs: others should be safe from both
enough of a lie, says the report

myth: the hadith gives three choices: good, true, or silent
it gives two: say what is good, or keep silent.
a report in Muslim's introduction warns against passing on everything you hear
it calls that enough of a lie, even when you invented nothing.
the Qur'an asks believers to check a report before acting on it
in the chapter called The Private Apartments (49:6), so as not to harm people in ignorance.

fork.setup: a dramatic story about someone you know is going around your group chat. you can't tell if it's true. what fits the saying in Muslim's introduction and 49:6?
options: share it with "not sure if this is true" on top.
pass it on to just a few close friends.
pass on nothing until you know it's true.
fork.reveal: the saying calls it enough of a lie to pass on everything you hear, and 49:6 asks for checking first. a disclaimer or a small audience is still passing it on.

original.note: Arabic: the tongue, and also a language or a way of speaking.

trapdoor: what you thought: online speech has its own rules.
what it means: the old adab of speech applies to every post: say good or stay silent, keep your hand as safe as your tongue, check before you share.

what a scholar hears: Bukhari's 'say good or keep silent' and 'safe from his tongue and his hand', the warning in the introduction to Sahih Muslim, and 49:6 and 49:12 on checking reports and backbiting.

notes: Confirm hadith references: Bukhari 6018; Bukhari 10 (the wording names 'Muslims' as those kept safe); the saying in the introduction to Sahih Muslim (numbered 5 in some editions).
49:6 and 49:12 are paraphrased, not quoted. 'The Private Apartments' is Pickthall's name for surah 49; confirm.
'Once, those were two different things' is the script's own observation about tongue and hand, not a sourced claim; a Keeper may soften it.
Week end (days 1387–1393): the teach closes with a one-line look back at this week's lines.
howItsDone is phrased with some teachers, not a general claim.

Editor: the hook's 'every word had a face in front of it' became a softer, unsourced-claim-free line; the fork had three options that were all forms of passing the rumor on, so the right answer is now 'pass on nothing until you know', tied to Muslim's introduction and 49:6.
